newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila targets transport and monetary reform.
newsitem.headline: Kabila targets transport and monetary reform.

text.p: President Laurent Kabila targeted transport and monetary reform in his inauguration address on Thursday and said his administration would aim to eradicate unemployment.

But his address, which concentrated more on political change under the third republic since independence from Belgium in 1960, did not go into whether his administration would pursue market-oriented reforms as a means to this end.

"We must rebuild the state so that it is able to play its role in the management of the country," he told a crowd of tens of thousands of supporters and curious Kinshasa residents in the capital's huge Chinese-built sports stadium.
"We must tackle the rehabilitation of all our social and economic infrastructures, particularly transport, which is a condition for for development," he said.
"We must drive out unemployment," he added, to the most enthusiastic burst of applause of the afternoon.
"To achieve all this programme we will also reunify our country on the monetary level -- we plan to replace the new zaire with a cleansed Congolese franc," he said.

No unemployment figures are available for the nation of well over 40 million people but economists guestimate that it is well over 70 percent. Many people scratch a living in the informal sector, trading anything from cigarettes to home-grown fruit or vegetables.
In the 1960s, the old Congolese franc was strong against the dollar. Ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko changed the currency to the zaire in 1967.
Kabila denounced Mobutu's three decades in power as "a period of irresponsible pillage, generalised corruption, institutionalised embezzlement, violence and flagrant violations of human rights".
This, he said, had undermined the the economic, social and moral fabric of Africa's third largest country.
Kabila's finance minister told reporters on Wednesday the Democratic Republic of Congo would print no new bank notes until the Congolese franc was introduced.

Mawampanga Mwanananga also said the government would set up special commissions to audit its hefty internal and external debt as a prelude to informal talks and then a conference with the country's creditors.
"It is important that the outside world knows that we are ready to make sacrifices to relaunch our economy," he said.
The minister gave no timing for the currrency switch. "Monetary reform is conducted to the surprise of everyone to avoid speculation," he said.
Ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko and successive governments under him printed money whenever they needed it, fuelling hyper- inflation which topped 8,000 percent in 1993.
A one stage, Zaire had three currency zones with different versions of the zaire trading a different rates.
The new zaire currently trades at 120,000 to the U.S. dollar on the parallel market in the capital Kinshasa.
The government fixed the official rate last Friday at 125,000. It plans to fix the rate every Friday.
